name: Battle of Zama
info: A Roman army under Scipio Africanus defeated a Carthaginian army under Hannibal near Zama in what is now Tunisia in 202 BCE, ending the Second Punic War and leaving Carthage politically subordinate to Rome.

facts.place: Near the town of Zama in what is now Tunisia; the site is generally, but not universally, believed to be a flat area south of Sicca (modern El Kef), the Draa el Metnan
facts.sides: Rome and its Numidian allies under Scipio Africanus and Masinissa, 29,000 or 30,000 by the usual modern figures, or approximately 40,000 (Bagnall); Carthage under Hannibal, 40,000 by most modern accounts following Polybius, or 50,000 by Appian, with 80 war elephants
facts.outcome: The Carthaginian army was routed when the Roman cavalry returned and charged its rear. Polybius puts Carthaginian dead at 20,000, with as many again captured, and Roman dead at 1,500. Carthage then accepted peace terms imposed by Rome.

t: Figures for both armies are uncertain: the Romans are usually given as 29,000 or 30,000 (Bagnall says 40,000) and the Carthaginians as 40,000 on Polybius's authority, against Appian's 50,000.
The Roman cavalry, sent from the field in pursuit of the Carthaginian horse, returned during the final infantry fight and charged the Carthaginian line in the rear.
The peace treaty took Carthage's overseas territories and some African ones, set an indemnity of 10,000 silver talents over 50 years and barred it from war without Rome's permission.
dyk: Hannibal's army had left its horses in Italy for lack of shipping space, and Hannibal also had to wait to train his elephants, so he met Scipio with only about 4,000 cavalry.
ev: Hannibal besieges, captures and sacks Saguntum, and early the next year Rome declares war on Carthage
Hannibal leads an army through Gaul and over the Alps into Italy
Scipio is elected consul and given Sicily as his province, with permission to cross to Africa on his own judgement
The Roman army lands near Utica and besieges it
Scipio's night attacks destroy the Numidian and Carthaginian camps, and Carthage recalls Hannibal and Mago from Italy
Scipio's army defeats Hannibal's near Zama
Carthage accepts the peace treaty imposed by Rome
Rome destroys Carthage at the end of the Third Punic War

sections.background:
The First Punic War, fought between Carthage and Rome from 264 to 241 BCE, lasted 23 years and ended in a Carthaginian defeat. Carthage expanded its territory in Iberia from 236 BCE, and in 226 BCE agreed the Ebro Treaty with Rome, which made the Ebro the northern boundary of the Carthaginian sphere of influence. Rome then made a treaty of association with Saguntum, well south of the river. Hannibal, the de facto ruler of Carthaginian Iberia, besieged, captured and sacked it in 219 BCE, and early the next year Rome declared war.

Hannibal invaded Italy in 218 BCE and inflicted heavy defeats on the Romans at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae, where at least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured. Toni Ñaco del Hoyo calls these "great military calamities", and Brian Carey writes that they brought Rome to the brink of collapse. In Iberia, Publius Cornelius Scipio took command of the Roman forces in 210 BCE and drove the Carthaginians out in 206 BCE.

Scipio was elected consul in early 205 BCE at the age of 31, when the minimum age was 42. Roman opinion was divided on whether an invasion of North Africa was an excessive risk, since Hannibal was still in Italy and the Romans had been driven out of Africa in 256 BCE. The compromise gave Scipio Sicily as his province and permission to cross to Africa on his own judgement, but he could only call for volunteers.
sections.forces:
The army that Scipio took to Africa had four legions, each of the Roman pair reinforced to an unprecedented 6,200 infantry, with 300 cavalry each. Modern historians estimate 25,000 to 30,000 men, including perhaps 2,500 cavalry. The core was the survivors of Cannae, formed into two legions and sent to Sicily, and Scipio trained the army for approximately a year. At Zama the ancient sources agree that 6,000 Numidian infantry and 4,000 cavalry under Masinissa supported it. Appian gives 34,500 in all, which modern historians do not accept. They usually give 29,000 or 30,000, though Nigel Bagnall gives 40,000.

Carthage normally recruited foreigners, many of them from North Africa and called Libyans. Appian states that its army at Zama numbered 50,000, which many modern historians discount; most give 40,000 on Polybius's authority, all but 4,000 of them infantry. Hannibal also had 80 war elephants. His army was made up of the survivors of three armies and he deployed them separately. Light infantry, then the elephants, stood in front of three infantry lines: troops of Mago's expedition, Carthaginians and Africans of poor morale or little training, and about 200 metres behind them Hannibal's veterans from Italy, estimated at 12,000, 15,000 to 20,000 or 20,000.

Scipio set a principes maniple directly behind each hastati maniple, leaving broad avenues for the velites. Masinissa's cavalry stood on the right and Gaius Laelius led 1,500 Roman and allied cavalry on the left.
sections.course:
The first clashes were between the Numidian cavalry on the Carthaginian left and Masinissa's on the Roman right. Hannibal then sent his 80 elephants against the Roman infantry, with his first two lines following. The velites threw javelins at the elephants and fell back, and the Roman infantry sounded bugles. Several elephants on the left fled through the Carthaginian cavalry, and Masinissa charged and routed it. Most of the others ran into the gaps between the Roman maniples, where javelins were thrown into their flanks, and those that came out behind the Roman army were hunted down. Some did charge the hastati and caused heavy casualties. Laelius likewise charged the disordered Carthaginian cavalry on the right and swept it from the field.

The Roman heavy infantry and the first two Carthaginian lines then fought hand to hand. The Roman first line broke the Carthaginian front rank, but the second, whom Polybius describes as fighting "fanatically and in an extraordinary manner", pushed the hastati back until the principes joined in. Hannibal's third line did not counter-attack. The Romans recalled their pursuing hastati and extended their line to match the longer Carthaginian one.

The two lines charged "with the greatest fire and fury" in Polybius's words, and neither gained the advantage for some time. Then the cavalry of Masinissa and Laelius returned and charged the Carthaginian rear. The line collapsed in a great massacre, and Hannibal was one of the few Carthaginians to escape.
sections.aftermath:
Polybius states that 20,000 Carthaginians were killed and as many again taken prisoner, which accounts for the entire Carthaginian army, and gives Roman losses as 1,500 killed. At least 11 Carthaginian elephants were captured. Hannibal and his surviving companions reached Hadrumetum, where they mustered 6,000 infantry and 500 cavalry. Considering this too few to continue the war, he advised the Carthaginian Senate to make peace on whatever terms it could get.

The Romans looted the Carthaginian camp and Scipio marched back to Tunis. During the talks a Numidian army under Vermina, the son of Syphax, was intercepted and defeated by a mostly cavalry force; Livy records that more than 16,000 were killed or captured. This was the last battle of the Second Punic War.

The treaty stripped Carthage of its overseas territories and some African ones. It set an indemnity of 10,000 silver talents, to be paid over 50 years, took hostages, forbade war elephants, limited the fleet to 10 warships and prohibited war outside Africa, and in Africa without Rome's express permission. Many senior Carthaginians wanted to reject it, but Hannibal spoke strongly in its favour and it was accepted in spring 201 BCE. Scipio was awarded a triumph and the agnomen Africanus.
sections.sources:
The main source for almost every aspect of the Punic Wars is Polybius, a Greek sent to Rome as a hostage in 167 BCE, who wrote The Histories sometime after 146 BCE. His work is considered broadly objective and largely neutral between Carthaginian and Roman points of view, and he interviewed participants from both sides where he could. Modern historians think he treated the relatives of his patron and friend Scipio Aemilianus unduly favourably, but the consensus is to accept his account largely at face value. Much of his account of the Second Punic War survives only in fragments.

Livy relied heavily on Polybius and is used where Polybius is missing, although Adrian Goldsworthy says his reliability is often suspect and Philip Sabin refers to his military ignorance. Dexter Hoyos describes Livy's account of Zama as bizarrely at odds with Polybius's. Appian and Cassius Dio are described by John Lazenby as clearly far inferior to Livy, and Hoyos accuses Appian of bizarre invention at Zama. Other sources include coins, inscriptions and archaeological evidence.

Much remains uncertain. The site is generally, but not universally, placed at the Draa el Metnan. Little is known of Scipio's numbers, and the ancient sources do not say what role the 6,000 Numidian infantry took. Historians disagree on whether the elephants were ill-advised, and on whether the Carthaginian second line withdrew deliberately.
sections.legacy:
The defeat left Carthage with no army with which to continue the war. The treaty made Carthage clearly subordinate to Rome, and Scipio took the agnomen Africanus.

The prohibition on waging war without Rome's permission had lasting effects. Masinissa repeatedly raided and seized Carthaginian territory with impunity, and Carthage's appeals to Rome were always backed by Rome's Numidian ally. In 149 BCE, fifty years after the Second Punic War ended, Carthage sent an army under Hasdrubal the Boetharch against Masinissa despite the treaty. The campaign ended in disaster at the Battle of Oroscopa, and anti-Carthaginian factions in Rome used the unauthorised action as a pretext to prepare a punitive expedition.

The Third Punic War began later in 149 BCE when a large Roman army landed in North Africa and besieged Carthage. In the spring of 146 BCE the Romans launched their final assault, systematically destroying the city and killing its inhabitants; 50,000 survivors were sold into slavery. The former Carthaginian territories were annexed by Rome and made the province of Africa, with Utica as its capital.

summary: At Zama in 202 BCE Scipio's Roman and Numidian army defeated Hannibal's Carthaginian army, and the Roman cavalry's charge on its rear decided the fight. Carthage accepted a treaty that left it subordinate to Rome, and Rome destroyed the city in 146 BCE.
references: Brian Todd Carey, Hannibal's Last Battle: Zama & the Fall of Carthage (Pen & Sword, 2007)
Mir Bahmanyar, Zama 202 BC: Scipio Crushes Hannibal in North Africa (Osprey, 2016)
John Lazenby, Hannibal's War: A Military History of the Second Punic War (Aris & Phillips, 1998)
Adrian Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage: The Punic Wars 265–146 BC (Phoenix, 2006)
Dexter Hoyos, Mastering the West: Rome and Carthage at War (Oxford University Press, 2015)
notes: The article gives no day or month for the battle, only 202 BC.

Contradiction in the article: the lead says Hannibal campaigned in Italy for 16 years, the Background 14 years, another section 12 years by 207 BC; I gave no duration. Iberia: lead says Scipio cleared it in five years, Background four years; I gave only the dates 210 and 206.
Roman strength: the lead says approximately 40,000, the Numbers section 29,000 or 30,000 (Bagnall 40,000), Appian 34,500. I gave all of them in facts and takeaways.
Carthaginian third line has three estimates, all given. The 6,000 Numidian infantry's role is unknown. The elephants' placement differs between most accounts and Lago.
The lead says Hannibal was forced into exile; the article does not describe it elsewhere, so I left it out.
Roman casualties of 1,500 and Carthaginian 20,000 killed and 20,000 captured are Polybius's only; no other figures are given.

Left out: Scipio's night attacks details beyond the event line, Cirta, Mago's death, the Roman raids selling inhabitants of towns into slavery (the prelude), Syphax's capture. The article's legacy material is thin, so the legacy section rests on the treaty and the Third Punic War.
